The King James Bible is a sixteen eleven English translation of the Hebrew Bible and Christian New Testament commissioned by King James I of England. Its majestic, cadent prose established a register of English that would dominate religious and literary thought for centuries, becoming the most influential translation in the English-speaking world and shaping the language itself through thousands of phrases now embedded in vernacular speech.

Forty-seven translators worked in teams for over a decade to complete it. They translated from the Textus Receptus, the Greek New Testament, and Hebrew Massoretic texts available at the time, not the earliest or most reliable manuscripts. The result is famous for its rhythmic, archaic English. "In the beginning was the Word" and "I am the resurrection and the life" became canonical phrasings. The Bible introduced or cemented hundreds of phrases in English now taken for granted: salt of the earth, the writing on the wall, go the extra mile, knock and it shall be opened unto you.

The Geneva Bible, published in fifteen sixty, was the scholarly alternative favored by Protestants, but the King James Version was less scholarly and far more resonant and eventually superseded it. The text underwent fifty-four authorized editions with minor corrections between sixteen eleven and seventeen sixty-nine, with the Blayney revision becoming the standard modern text. The King James Bible was challenged in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries by newer translations using earlier manuscripts, such as the Revised Version and the Revised Standard Version, yet it remains culturally dominant.
